title: Direction and Execution
author: Dr. Ian Hallett
summary: In part two of his five-part Leadership Operating System series, Ian Hallett examines the Direction and Execution domain: making goals and priorities clear, making sure commitments are delivered, and putting time, people and money behind what matters. He opens with Steve Jobs cutting Apple from fifteen product lines to four and returning it to profit on lower revenue, then cites research on laissez-faire leadership and goal-setting to show that silence from a leader makes teams less clear and less effective. His central tool is a weekly thirty-minute meeting built on three questions: what are we trying to achieve and what wins in a conflict, what did we say we would do and is it done, and what are we stopping or moving to make room. He breaks the domain into fifteen concrete behaviours across clarity, accountability and prioritisation, and names four common failure patterns: the everything priority, the add-on, the green report and the heroic finish. The point for capable operators is that the leadership question shifts from whether you can get it done to whether the team does when you are not watching.
points: A weekly half-hour with three questions (what wins, what is done, what stops) converts clarity, accountability and prioritisation into a routine that runs without the leader.
A priority is only clear if someone can use it to choose between two pieces of work without asking the leader, so rank three or four in writing and explain the reasoning behind decisions.
Prioritisation is proven by where time, people and money actually moved, so compare ranked priorities to real spending each month and name what stops whenever something new starts.
Rescuing a slipping deadline yourself feels like leadership but teaches the team that dates are soft and leaves the cause unfixed.
Asking only whether things are on track produces green reports until it is too late to help; agree checkpoint dates and close every decision with who does what by when.
quotes: So Apple returned to profit while selling less. What had changed was what the company was trying to do, and what it had stopped paying for.
The question changes from whether you can get it done to whether your team gets it done when you are not watching.
Clarity is what your team uses when you are away. A priority is only clear if someone can use it to choose between two pieces of work without asking you.
The reason is what lets someone do the right thing when the situation changes and you cannot be asked.
Prioritisation is where clarity gets paid for. The test of a priority is whether time, people and money moved when you named it.
The add-on. New work announced on top of old, with nothing moved and nothing stopped. The extra capacity comes from people’s evenings, and the team knows it before you do.

The heroic finish. We see a deadline slipping and fix it ourselves, late at night. It works, it feels like leadership, and it teaches the team that dates are soft because you will catch whatever falls.
